prompt: When a nucleophile adds to a carboxylic acid derivative, what does the tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate usually do next?

choices.text: It expels a leaving group to give a new carbonyl compound
It is protonated to give an alcohol
choices.why: That is what happens with aldehydes and ketones, which have no leaving group. Their reaction is a nucleophilic addition.

choices.text: It stays as the final, stable product
choices.why: The intermediate doesn't last. In an acid derivative it quickly expels the –Y group and re-forms the C=O.

choices.text: It loses its alkoxide oxygen as hydroxide ion
choices.why: The alkoxide oxygen stays and re-forms the C=O double bond as the –Y group is expelled.

explanation: Both nucleophilic addition and nucleophilic acyl substitution start with addition to the polar C=O to give a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate. From an aldehyde or ketone the intermediate is protonated to an alcohol, but from a carboxylic acid derivative it expels a leaving group to give a new carbonyl compound (Figure 21.2.1).

prompt: Why don't aldehydes and ketones undergo nucleophilic acyl substitution?

choices.text: They have no group on the carbonyl carbon that can leave
Nucleophiles can't add to the C=O bond of an aldehyde or ketone
choices.why: Nucleophiles add readily to aldehydes and ketones. That is nucleophilic addition.

choices.text: Their carbonyl groups are not polar enough to attract a nucleophile
choices.why: The C=O bond of an aldehyde or ketone is polar, just like that of an acid derivative.

choices.text: They don't form a tetrahedral intermediate when a nucleophile adds
choices.why: They do form a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate, which is then protonated to give an alcohol.

explanation: Carboxylic acid derivatives have an acyl carbon bonded to a group –Y that can act as a leaving group, often as a stable anion. Aldehydes and ketones have only –H or –R on the carbonyl carbon, which don't leave, so they don't undergo substitution.

prompt: How does a nucleophilic acyl substitution differ from an S_N2 reaction?

choices.text: It takes place in two steps through a tetrahedral intermediate, while S_N2 is a one-step backside displacement
It takes place in one step by backside displacement, like S_N2 but at an sp2 carbon
choices.why: One-step backside displacement describes S_N2. Acyl substitution is an addition followed by an elimination.

choices.text: It goes through a carbocation formed when the leaving group departs before the nucleophile adds
choices.why: Losing the leaving group first describes S_N1. In acyl substitution the nucleophile adds first.

choices.text: Its net result is different, because the nucleophile is lost and the leaving group stays
choices.why: The net results are similar: the nucleophile replaces the leaving group. Only the mechanisms differ.

explanation: The overall result looks like an S_N2 substitution, but the mechanisms are completely different. An S_N2 reaction occurs in a single step by backside displacement, while a nucleophilic acyl substitution takes place in two steps and involves a tetrahedral intermediate.

prompt: Which step is usually rate-limiting in a nucleophilic acyl substitution reaction?

choices.text: Addition of the nucleophile to the carbonyl group
Expulsion of the leaving group from the tetrahedral intermediate
choices.why: Both steps can affect the rate, but the section says the addition is usually the rate-limiting step.

choices.text: Protonation of the alkoxide oxygen
choices.why: In acyl substitution the alkoxide isn't protonated. It re-forms the C=O as the leaving group departs.

choices.text: Loss of the leaving group before the nucleophile arrives
choices.why: No leaving group departs before the nucleophile adds. The order is addition first, then elimination.

explanation: Both the addition and the elimination step can affect the rate, but the addition is usually rate-limiting. So any factor that makes the carbonyl group more reactive toward nucleophiles favors the substitution.

prompt: Which list puts these acid derivatives in order of increasing reactivity toward nucleophilic acyl substitution?

choices.text: Amide < ester < thioester < acid anhydride < acid chloride
Acid chloride < acid anhydride < thioester < ester < amide
choices.why: This is the reverse order. Acid chlorides are the most reactive and amides the least.

choices.text: Amide < thioester < ester < acid anhydride < acid chloride
choices.why: In the section's order, thioesters are more reactive than esters, not less.

choices.text: Ester < amide < thioester < acid chloride < acid anhydride
choices.why: Amides are the least reactive derivatives, and acid chlorides are the most reactive.

explanation: Figure 21.2.2 ranks the derivatives from least to most reactive: amide < ester < thioester < acid anhydride < acid chloride. A more reactive derivative can be converted into a less reactive one, but not the reverse.

prompt: Why are acid chlorides the most reactive carboxylic acid derivatives?

choices.text: Electronegative chlorine withdraws electrons from the carbonyl carbon
Chlorine donates electrons to the carbonyl group by resonance
choices.why: Chlorine withdraws electrons inductively. Resonance donation is what amino, methoxyl, and methylthio groups do, and it lowers reactivity.

choices.text: The carbonyl carbon of an acid chloride is more sterically hindered
choices.why: Steric hindrance slows reactions; it couldn't explain high reactivity. The reason is electronic.

choices.text: Acid chlorides are the least polarized acid derivatives
choices.why: Acid chlorides are the most strongly polarized acid derivatives, and that is why they are the most reactive.

explanation: Strongly polarized acyl compounds react more readily than less polar ones. The electronegative chlorine inductively withdraws electrons from the carbonyl carbon, so acid chlorides are the most reactive. Electrostatic potential maps show this as a bluer (more positive) C=O carbon.

prompt: How do amino, methoxyl, and methylthio substituents affect the reactivity of an acyl group toward nucleophiles?

choices.text: They donate electrons by resonance, making the acyl group less reactive
They withdraw electrons inductively, making the acyl group more reactive
choices.why: Inductive withdrawal is how a chlorine substituent acts. These groups donate electrons by resonance.

choices.text: They donate electrons by resonance, making the acyl group more reactive
choices.why: Electron donation makes the carbonyl carbon less electron-poor, so it is less reactive toward nucleophiles. That's why amides and esters are less reactive than acid chlorides.

choices.text: They have no effect, because only steric factors matter
choices.why: Both steric and electronic factors determine reactivity.

explanation: Substituents affect an acyl group much as they affect an aromatic ring (Section 16.4). Amino, methoxyl, and methylthio groups donate electrons to the acyl group by resonance, which reduces the polarization of the carbonyl group and makes amides, esters, and thioesters less reactive than acid chlorides.

prompt: Where do acyl phosphates fit on the reactivity scale of carboxylic acid derivatives, according to the section?

choices.text: They appear to be somewhat more reactive than thioesters
They are more reactive than acid chlorides
choices.why: The section doesn't place them above acid chlorides. It says only that they seem somewhat more reactive than thioesters.

choices.text: They appear to be somewhat less reactive than amides
choices.why: Amides are the least reactive derivatives. Acyl phosphates appear more reactive than thioesters.

choices.text: They appear to be exactly as reactive as esters
choices.why: The section says they are hard to place but seem somewhat more reactive than thioesters, which are already more reactive than esters.

explanation: Acyl phosphates are hard to place on the reactivity scale because they are not often used in the laboratory, but in biological systems they appear to be somewhat more reactive than thioesters.

prompt: Which conversion can be carried out directly by nucleophilic acyl substitution?

choices.text: An acid chloride into an amide
An amide into an ester
choices.why: Amides are the least reactive derivatives, and a less reactive derivative can't be converted directly into a more reactive one.

choices.text: An ester into an acid chloride
choices.why: Acid chlorides are more reactive than esters, so this would go uphill on the reactivity scale.

choices.text: An amide into an acid anhydride
choices.why: Amides can't be converted directly into esters, thioesters, anhydrides, or acid chlorides.

explanation: A more reactive acid derivative can be converted into a less reactive one, but not vice versa (Figure 21.2.2). Acid chlorides can be converted directly into anhydrides, thioesters, esters, and amides.

prompt: Why aren't acid halides and acid anhydrides found in living organisms?

choices.text: They react so rapidly with water that they can't exist for long
They are too unreactive to take part in biological reactions
choices.why: The opposite is true. They are the two most reactive derivatives.

choices.text: Organisms can't make the carboxylic acids they would come from
choices.why: Carboxylic acids are common in organisms. The problem is that these reactive derivatives don't survive in water.

choices.text: They don't undergo nucleophilic acyl substitution
choices.why: They undergo nucleophilic acyl substitution very readily, including with water.

explanation: Only acyl phosphates, thioesters, esters, and amides are commonly found in nature. Acid halides and acid anhydrides react so rapidly with water that they can't exist for long in living organisms.

prompt: Within a series of similar acid derivatives, which carbonyl groups react with nucleophiles more readily?

choices.text: Unhindered, accessible carbonyl groups
Sterically hindered carbonyl groups
choices.why: Bulky groups get in the way of the nucleophile, so hindered carbonyl groups react more slowly.

choices.text: Carbonyl groups bonded to strong electron-donating groups
choices.why: Electron donation reduces the polarization of the carbonyl group and makes it less reactive.

choices.text: Carbonyl groups with no leaving group attached
choices.why: Without a leaving group, as in aldehydes and ketones, substitution can't happen at all.

explanation: Sterically, unhindered, accessible carbonyl groups react with nucleophiles more readily than sterically hindered ones. Electronically, strongly polarized acyl compounds react more readily than less polar ones.

prompt: What is the reaction of a carboxylic acid derivative with an alcohol to yield an ester called?

choices.text: Alcoholysis
Hydrolysis
choices.why: Hydrolysis is reaction with water to yield a carboxylic acid.

choices.text: Aminolysis
choices.why: Aminolysis is reaction with ammonia or an amine to yield an amide.

choices.text: Reduction
choices.why: Reduction is reaction with a hydride reducing agent to yield an aldehyde or an alcohol.

explanation: Figure 21.2.3 lists the reactions that keep coming up: hydrolysis (water, gives an acid), alcoholysis (alcohol, gives an ester), aminolysis (ammonia or amine, gives an amide), reduction (hydride, gives an aldehyde or alcohol), and Grignard reaction (gives a ketone or alcohol).

prompt: What is the product of the nucleophilic acyl substitution reaction of benzoyl chloride, C6H5COCl, with 2-propanol?

choices.text: Isopropyl benzoate
Propyl benzoate
choices.why: Propyl benzoate would come from 1-propanol. 2-Propanol puts an isopropyl group on the ester oxygen.

choices.text: Benzoic acid and 2-chloropropane
choices.why: The alcohol oxygen is the nucleophile and Cl− is the leaving group, so the alcohol's –OR group replaces chlorine on the acyl carbon. No C–Cl bond forms to the alcohol.

choices.text: Isopropyl phenyl ketone
choices.why: A ketone would need a carbon nucleophile. The alcohol bonds through oxygen, giving an ester.

explanation: Identify the leaving group (Cl− in an acid chloride) and the nucleophile (the alcohol), then replace one by the other. Benzoyl chloride and 2-propanol give isopropyl benzoate (Worked Example 21.2.1).

prompt: Benzoyl chloride reacts with sodium methoxide in methanol to give methyl benzoate. Which species are the nucleophile and the leaving group?

choices.text: Methoxide ion is the nucleophile; chloride ion is the leaving group
Chloride ion is the nucleophile; methoxide ion is the leaving group
choices.why: This is reversed. Methoxide adds to the carbonyl carbon, and chloride is expelled.

choices.text: Sodium ion is the nucleophile; chloride ion is the leaving group
choices.why: Na+ is a positive ion with no electrons to donate. The nucleophile is the methoxide anion.

choices.text: Methoxide ion is the nucleophile; the phenyl group is the leaving group
choices.why: The phenyl group stays bonded; the product methyl benzoate still contains the benzoyl group.

explanation: Methoxide ion adds to the carbonyl carbon of benzoyl chloride to give a tetrahedral intermediate, which eliminates chloride ion to give methyl benzoate (Exercise 21.2.1).

prompt: Methyl acetate, CH3CO2CH3, reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Which product contains the acetyl part of the ester?

choices.text: Sodium acetate, CH3CO2^− Na+
Acetaldehyde, CH3CHO
choices.why: An aldehyde would need a hydride nucleophile. Here hydroxide replaces the –OCH3 group.

choices.text: Methanol, CH3OH
choices.why: Methanol comes from the –OCH3 leaving group. It doesn't contain the acetyl part.

choices.text: Acetic anhydride, (CH3CO)2O
choices.why: An ester can't be converted into an anhydride this way, because anhydrides are more reactive than esters.

explanation: Hydroxide is the nucleophile and methoxide is the leaving group. In the basic solution the acetic acid formed ends up as its sodium salt, so the answer to Exercise 21.2.3 is CH3CO2^− Na+.

prompt: What product forms when acetyl chloride, CH3COCl, reacts with ammonia?

choices.text: Acetamide, CH3CONH2
Methylamine, CH3NH2
choices.why: The carbonyl group is kept. –NH2 replaces –Cl on the acyl carbon.

choices.text: Acetic acid, CH3CO2H
choices.why: Acetic acid would come from reaction with water (hydrolysis). Ammonia gives an amide (aminolysis).

choices.text: Chloroacetamide, ClCH2CONH2
choices.why: Chlorine is the leaving group and departs as Cl−. It doesn't end up on carbon.

explanation: Ammonia is the nucleophile and chloride is the leaving group, so the product is CH3CONH2, acetamide (Exercise 21.2.3). This is an aminolysis.

prompt: Acetic anhydride, (CH3CO)2O, reacts with sodium methoxide in methanol. What are the products?

choices.text: Methyl acetate, CH3CO2CH3, and sodium acetate, CH3CO2^− Na+
Two molecules of methyl acetate, CH3CO2CH3
choices.why: Only one acetyl group is transferred to methoxide. The other half of the anhydride is the leaving group, acetate ion.

choices.text: Dimethyl ether, CH3OCH3, and acetic acid, CH3CO2H
choices.why: Methoxide adds to a carbonyl carbon. No bond forms between two methyl groups through oxygen.

choices.text: Acetone, CH3COCH3, and sodium acetate, CH3CO2^− Na+
choices.why: A ketone would need a carbon nucleophile. Methoxide bonds through oxygen, giving an ester.

explanation: Methoxide adds to one carbonyl group of the anhydride, and acetate ion is expelled. The products are CH3CO2CH3 and CH3CO2^− Na+ (Exercise 21.2.3).

prompt: What product forms when the thioester CH3COSCH3 reacts with methylamine, CH3NH2?

choices.text: N-Methylacetamide, CH3CONHCH3
Methyl acetate, CH3CO2CH3
choices.why: Methylamine attacks through nitrogen, so the product is an amide, not an oxygen ester.

choices.text: Acetamide, CH3CONH2
choices.why: The amine nitrogen keeps its methyl group, so the amide is N-substituted.

choices.text: Dimethyl sulfide, CH3SCH3, and acetamide, CH3CONH2
choices.why: The –SCH3 group leaves as a unit. The nitrogen of methylamine, with its methyl group, bonds to the acyl carbon.

explanation: Methylamine is the nucleophile and the –SCH3 group is the leaving group. Thioesters are more reactive than amides, so the conversion goes downhill on the reactivity scale and gives CH3CONHCH3 (Exercise 21.2.3).

prompt: Which order ranks ethyl acetate, 2,2,2-trichloroethyl acetate (CH3CO2CH2CCl3), and hexafluoroisopropyl acetate (CH3CO2CH(CF3)2) from most to least reactive toward nucleophilic acyl substitution?

choices.text: Hexafluoroisopropyl acetate > 2,2,2-trichloroethyl acetate > ethyl acetate
Ethyl acetate > 2,2,2-trichloroethyl acetate > hexafluoroisopropyl acetate
choices.why: This is the reverse. Electron-withdrawing halogens make the acyl group more polarized and more reactive, so ethyl acetate, with none, is the least reactive.

choices.text: 2,2,2-Trichloroethyl acetate > hexafluoroisopropyl acetate > ethyl acetate
choices.why: The six fluorines of the hexafluoroisopropyl group withdraw electrons more strongly than three chlorines, so that ester is the most reactive.

choices.text: All three react at the same rate, because they are all acetates
choices.why: The groups on oxygen differ in how strongly they withdraw electrons, and that changes the polarization of the carbonyl group.

explanation: Strongly polarized acyl compounds react more readily. Electronegative halogens on the alkoxy group withdraw electrons, so the more strongly withdrawing the group, the more reactive the ester: hexafluoroisopropyl acetate > 2,2,2-trichloroethyl acetate > ethyl acetate (Exercise 21.2.2).

prompt: A tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate, C5H9CH2C(O^−)(OH)(OCH3) where C5H9 is cyclopentyl, formed when hydroxide ion added to an ester. Which ester was the starting material?

choices.text: Methyl cyclopentylacetate, C5H9CH2CO2CH3
Cyclopentyl acetate, CH3CO2C5H9
choices.why: In that ester the ring is on the oxygen. In the intermediate, the ring is joined through a CH2 to the former carbonyl carbon.

choices.text: Methyl cyclopentanecarboxylate, C5H9CO2CH3
choices.why: That ester has no CH2 between the ring and the carbonyl carbon.

choices.text: Ethyl cyclopentylacetate, C5H9CH2CO2CH2CH3
choices.why: The intermediate carries an –OCH3 group, so the ester was a methyl ester.

explanation: The –OH came from the hydroxide nucleophile, and the –OCH3 group is the leaving group. Remove the hydroxide and restore the C=O to get the starting ester, C5H9CH2CO2CH3. Expelling methoxide gives the carboxylic acid (Exercise 21.2.4).
